issues.issue: The preamble directs the reader to "Section 8 of this Agreement" for capitalized definitions, but Section 8 is "Legal Matters" and the definitions are in Section 9. That is a mechanical cross-reference error on the face of the provision.

The cross-reference cannot be squared with Section 9 ("Definitions"), which is where the defined terms actually live. A court asked which terms are defined and where would have to fix the misdirection.

The statement that the Corporation "desires to assure itself of Executive's employment" sits uneasily with Section 5(a)'s at-will disclaimer, but it is a purpose recital rather than an operative promise. The tension is mild.

"[O]r in another management position assigned to Executive by the Corporation's Board of Directors" sets no floor on what position may be assigned, leaving the scope of the employment promise indeterminate. The phrase carries more than one reasonable reading.

The Corporation's freedom to move Executive to "another management position" is hard to reconcile with Section 9(d)(ii), which makes a material reduction of Executive's duties, responsibilities or title "Good Reason". A reassignment permitted by Section 3 could be a Good Reason event under Section 9(d).

"The next salary adjustment is scheduled for April 1, 2015" does not say whether an adjustment is promised or merely calendared for discretionary review, and the preceding sentence makes any adjustment discretionary. The word "scheduled" carries both readings.

Board discretion to adjust Base Salary sits against Section 9(d)(iii), which makes a significant reduction of Base Salary "Good Reason". The two provisions must be harmonised to know whether downward adjustment is permitted.

The clause grants a "right to receive an annual bonus" of a fixed $140,000 yet conditions it on remaining "an employee of the Corporation in good standing on the date of payment" and on satisfying KPIs the Corporation itself sets; "good standing" is undefined and the entitlement is at once fixed and discretionary. It also calls a sum an "annual bonus" while directing that it be paid "semi-annually", leaving the amount per payment uncertain.

The bonus right cannot be squared with Section 5(b), under which all rights to bonuses that would have become payable after termination cease, and with Section 18, which makes all of Section 4 survive termination. Whether a bonus earned before but payable after termination is owed turns on that clash.

The matching contribution commences "at such time when the Company is able to make such matching contribution under the Plan", a trigger with no objective standard and wholly within the payor's control. "[A]ble to" is the term that cannot be applied at its boundary.

The paragraph refers to "the Company" although the defined party throughout the Agreement is "the Corporation", leaving the obligor of the Contribution Start Date trigger unnamed. The mismatch shows only against the preamble's definition.

Eligibility to participate in the "Stock Option Plan" is made "subject to approval by the Board and the Corporation's policies", so it is arguable whether anything at all was promised. The Stock Option Plan is also never identified.

The clause declares Executive "at-will" and terminable "for any reason or no reason" while simultaneously entitling him to ninety days' prior notice if terminated without Cause, and then denies any contract "for any particular period of time". Whether the ninety-day notice is an enforceable entitlement or is overridden by the at-will language is exactly the kind of question two parties read differently.

The clause twice refers to the termination date "specified in accordance with this Section 4" although the termination provisions are Section 5, and it makes no provision for the "Good Reason" resignation defined in Section 9(d). Both cross-instrument gaps must be resolved before the notice mechanics can be applied.

The carve-out for "other amounts owing under the Corporation's standard, Board-approved policies" is a general catch-all trailing two specifics (vested retirement benefits, accrued insurance benefits), so its reach over items such as accrued bonus is uncertain. The catch-all's boundary is the disputed term.

The cut-off of post-termination compensation conflicts with Section 18, which makes Section 4 (Compensation and Benefits) survive termination "in full force and effect", and with the Annual Bonus right in Section 4(b). Harmonising them still leaves a genuine inconsistency about accrued but unpaid bonus.
"[B]ona fide amounts not in dispute" is undefined and self-referential — a party need only dispute an amount to defeat the offset. The boundary of "not in dispute" is the term at issue.

"[T]he Business" is defined by an enumerated list of software and IT services with no catch-all, so activities adjacent to but outside the list fall outside every covenant keyed to "the Business". The list's scope drives the non-compete's reach.

This warranty duplicates, and is narrower than, the representation in Section 7(ii) that Executive is not bound by any employment, non-compete or confidentiality agreement. The overlap is redundancy rather than contradiction.

The restriction bars "any new transactions, deals or relations of any kind including but not limited to" a list of specific acts, so the catch-all's reach against the enumerated specifics is genuinely uncertain, and "inconsistent, or incompatible with interests or obligations of the Corporation" has no ascertainable boundary. The sentence's mangled syntax makes the object of each verb arguable.

The covenant runs for the "Term of this Agreement" plus twenty-four months, but "Term" is nowhere defined in the instrument (Section 9 defines no such term), and "Affiliate" is given one meaning here (Section 6, ten percent ownership) and a different one in Section 9(a). Both must be resolved before the covenant's duration and reach can be fixed.

"[I]nterfere with or damage (or attempt to interfere with or damage) any relationship" sets no standard for what conduct counts, and the covenant applies to "Client" as broadly defined including mere prospects. The reach of the interference limb is the contestable term.

The twenty-four month tail runs from "the Term of this Agreement", an undefined term, and depends on the Section 6 "Affiliate" definition, which differs from Section 9(a)'s. Duration and covered entities cannot be fixed from this clause alone.

"Solicit" is defined to include "any direct or indirect communication of any kind whatsoever, regardless of by whom initiated", which sweeps in responding to an unsolicited approach and is arguably no limit at all. Whether "advising" or "encouraging" covers passive conduct is the disputed edge.

The definition is circular — "Client" means "any customer, Client or prospective client" — and extends to any person "whose identity became known to the Executive", a boundary that cannot be applied. The circularity and the knowledge limb are both nameable defects.

The definition includes "members of the Family of such Person", capitalising "Family" as though defined when it is defined nowhere in the Agreement. The class of persons swept in is therefore indeterminate.

This Section 6 definition of "Affiliate" (ten percent ownership, or control, of any Person) is materially different from the Section 9(a) definition (entities controlling, controlled by or under common control with the Corporation). A court applying "Affiliate" must choose between two operative definitions in the same instrument.

This Section 6 definition of "Person" overlaps with, but is not identical to, the Section 12(e) definition of "person", which adds groups, syndicates, cooperatives and governmental subdivisions. The two lists could be read differently on the same facts.

"[T]he abovementioned provision" has no identified antecedent — it could mean the Non-Solicitation of Clients covenant, the Conflict of Interest covenant, or all of Section 6. The reference is the ambiguity.

The general damages right here overlaps the more detailed "Remedies" paragraph of Section 6, which already grants recovery of profits and damages, and the fixed $50,000 damages in the employee non-solicitation paragraph. Whether these remedies are cumulative or alternative is not stated.

The exception "unless prior written consent is given by the Executive" is plainly a mechanical error — the Executive consenting to his own solicitation would nullify the covenant, and the consent must have been meant to come from the Corporation. The error changes what the provision means.

The $50,000 per employee "fixed damages" cannot easily be reconciled with the immediately preceding damages paragraph and with the "Remedies" paragraph of Section 6, which entitles the Corporation to all profits and "any damages suffered". Whether the liquidated sum is exclusive or additive is left open.

"Confidential Information" is defined by "includes", which Section 12(a) makes "always without limitation", so the category has no outer edge and covers "all information and materials belonging to, used by, or in the possession of the Corporation". The open-endedness is the defect.

The definitional sentence has unbalanced parentheses and runs the "Assigned Inventions"/"Retained Inventions" carve-outs together, so it is arguable whether inventions made "outside of his capacity as an employee" are retained or assigned. The grammatical break changes the scope of the assignment.

The carve-out depends on "the materials listed on Exhibit B attached hereto", but no Exhibit B is attached to the instrument (only Exhibit A). The Retained Inventions carve-out cannot be applied without it.

"[A]dequate and current written records of all inventions" uses "inventions" uncapitalised and unqualified, so it is unclear whether it reaches Retained Inventions made outside employment. The phrase "Assigned Inventions other than Retained Inventions" is also redundant on the Section 6 definitions.

The power-of-attorney sentence reads "[i]f the Corporation is unable because of the Corporation's mental or physical incapacity ... to secure the Corporation's signature", when the only person with mental or physical capacity and the signature needed is the Executive. The mechanical error inverts the condition on which the appointment operates.

The NDA is executed "[s]imultaneously herewith", yet Section 14 states that this Agreement "records the final, complete, and exclusive understanding" and supersedes any "contemporaneous agreement ... oral or written". Whether the integration clause displaces the NDA is a genuine internal problem.

The tolling sentence extends "[t]he duration of every restriction set forth in this section ... by any period during which the Executive is in breach", without saying who determines breach or when the period runs. The extension's operation is indeterminate.

The declaration that Executive's covenant obligations are "independent of any other obligation" including promises in this Agreement is in tension with the "Remedies" paragraph, which excuses the Corporation from its own obligations on breach. The two treat dependency of obligations in opposite ways.

"[A]ny public statement reflecting negatively" is a vague standard, and the covenant is one-sided (Executive only) with no reciprocal duty. "Reflecting negatively" is the term whose boundary would be argued.

The severability sentence refers to invalidity not affecting "any other provision of this letter", although the instrument is an Agreement, not a letter — a leftover mechanical error. It also purports to bind the Executive's acknowledgment that no further geographic narrowing would be appropriate.

This blue-pencil/severability paragraph duplicates and partly differs from the severability language in Section 11, which speaks only of covenants being "deemed separable". Which controls a covenant held excessively broad is not stated.

The forfeiture applies "if it breaches any of the covenants of this Agreement" — not merely the restrictive covenants — so any breach, however trivial, would excuse the Corporation from paying compensation. The reach of "any of the covenants" is the contestable term.

Excusing the Corporation from "paying or performing any liability or obligation owed to the Executive (including compensation)" cannot be squared with the unconditional payment obligations in Section 4 or with Section 6's statement that the covenants are independent of other obligations. The clash goes to whether earned wages can be forfeited.

The representation that Executive is bound by no "confidentiality agreement with any other person or entity" sits oddly beside the NDA executed simultaneously with the Corporation, though the Corporation is not another person. The tension is slight.
"[T]he losing party" and "the prevailing party" are undefined and unworkable where each side wins part of a claim. Who prevailed is the classic contested term in a fee-shifting clause.

The symmetrical fee-shift here is hard to reconcile with the "Remedies" paragraph of Section 6, which gives the Corporation reimbursement of all enforcement costs regardless of outcome. The two cost provisions point different ways.

This definition of "Affiliate" (control-based, keyed to the Corporation) contradicts the "Affiliate" definition in Section 6, which is keyed to ten percent ownership of any Person and includes family members. Two operative definitions of the same capitalised term govern the same covenants.

Limb (v) ends with the general catch-all "or breached this Agreement, or the NDA, or any material Corporation policy or other agreement", which swallows the four carefully enumerated grounds and makes any breach whatever a Cause event. The tension between the specific list and the catch-all is the defect.

Limb (v) refers to "the Restrictive Covenants set forth in Section 5 of this Agreement", but the Restrictive Covenants are Section 6 and Section 5 is Termination. The cross-reference cannot be reconciled with the body of the instrument.

Whether Executive is disabled is left "as determined by the Board in its good faith judgment", with a fallback standard turning on "reasonable accommodations" the Corporation itself decides. The determination mechanism is the contestable term.

Limb (i) repeats "or the Corporation is not otherwise diligently pursuing a remedy, within twenty-one (21) business days" twice in the same sentence, and limb (iii) omits any notice or cure step the other limbs require. The duplicated clause and asymmetric cure mechanics obscure when Good Reason arises.

"Good Reason" is defined in Section 9(d) but appears nowhere else in the instrument — Section 5 provides no severance or other consequence for a Good Reason resignation. The definition cannot be reconciled with a contract that gives it no operative effect.

This severability language overlaps the "Judicial Modification" paragraph of Section 6, which additionally authorises blue-pencilling of overbroad restrictions. Which governs an unenforceable restrictive covenant is unstated.

Section 9(d) measures its cure periods in "business days" while this provision defines "days" as calendar days, so the two day-counting conventions coexist in one instrument. The mismatch is mild but real.
This definition of "person" differs in scope from the capitalised "Person" defined in Section 6, and the two are used in overlapping contexts. A court would have to decide which list applies where.

Notices must be "addressed to the addresses for the parties listed below", but the signature page leaves Executive's address blank. The notice machinery — including the ninety-day notices required by Section 5(a) — cannot be operated as written.
